0.0.n: A conversational filler that softens the opening.

0.1.n: A polite way to refer to the item being shown.

0.2.n: Links the noun-like こちら to explanatory ん; it is the form of だ used before ん.

0.3.n: Short for の, adding an explanatory tone rather than naming anything.

0.4.n: Makes the explanation with ん polite.

0.5.n: Softens the introduction and keeps the conversation open, without necessarily expressing a contrast.

0.7.n: Names the item after pointing to it with こちら.

1.0.n: States the price; 円 is the Japanese currency unit.

1.1.n: Marks the price at which the ramen is available.

1.2.n: Names the food available through the promotion.

1.3.n: Marks ラーメン as the thing one can eat with the ability form 食べられる.

1.4.n: The ability form of 食べる; here it describes what the deal lets customers do.

1.5.n: Casual form of という, introducing the offer that describes the campaign in the next line.

1.7.n: Refers back to the offer just described.

1.8.n: Combines with 限定 to describe an offer available only during a set time.

1.9.n: Follows 期間 to make 期間限定, describing a temporary offer.

1.10.n: Connects 期間限定 to キャンペーン in the next line.

1.11.n: Adds a conversational pause while the speaker continues toward キャンペーン.

2.0.n: This borrowed word refers to a special sales offer, not a political campaign.

2.1.n: Short for やっていた, the past ongoing form of やる; the object marker を after キャンペーン is omitted.

2.2.n: Conversational shortening of ので, giving the promotion as background for the visit.

2.4.n: Softens how strongly the speaker expresses their curiosity.

2.5.n: Part of 気になる, an expression for something catching your interest or bothering you.

2.6.n: Connects 気 with なる in 気になる; it does not mark a destination here.

2.7.n: Past form of なる; together with 気に, it says the offer caught the speaker's interest.

2.8.n: Marks the speaker's curiosity as the reason for coming.

2.9.n: Polite past form of 来る, describing the speaker's arrival here.

3.0.n: A conversational connector that moves on to the next part of the account.

3.2.n: Refers to the ramen in front of the speaker; the object marker を is omitted.

3.3.n: A humble, polite alternative to 食べる; this form itself does not say the eating has already happened.

3.4.n: Short for explanatory の, framing the eating as context for what follows.

3.5.n: Makes the explanation with ん polite.

3.6.n: Leads gently into the following remarks rather than necessarily introducing a strong contrast.

4.0.n: Softens the speaker's assessment before giving an opinion.

4.1.n: Names the aspect of the ramen being evaluated.

4.2.n: は sets 味 as the topic, while ね adds a conversational touch.

4.4.n: Describes a familiar, standard product rather than something special.

4.5.n: Connects 普通 to the following brand name so it describes the product.

4.6.n: Part of the instant noodle brand name サッポロ一番, not a separate reference to the city here.

4.7.n: Part of the brand name サッポロ一番; literally means number one, but does not rank the ramen here.

4.8.n: Presents the brand as one example rather than a complete list.

4.9.n: Points back to the brand example and describes 即席ラーメン in the next line.

4.10.n: Keeps a conversational tone during a pause before the description continues.

5.0.n: Combines directly with ラーメン to name the quick-preparation noodle category.

5.1.n: Together with 即席, refers to packaged noodles prepared quickly.

5.2.n: Marks instant ramen as the thing being compared with this ramen's taste.

5.3.n: Used with と to compare the taste with instant ramen.

5.4.n: In 同じような, it makes the comparison approximate rather than strictly identical.

5.5.n: Connects よう to the noun 味 so the comparison describes the taste.

5.6.n: The noun described by the comparison 同じような.

5.7.n: Politely completes the statement after the noun 味.

5.8.n: Softens the assessment and invites the listener to share the impression.

0.lit: Well, it is this, you see, but—ramen.
0.tip: なんですけれども politely introduces something; the but-like ending need not signal a real contrast.

1.lit: For 150 yen, ramen can be eaten—that kind of limited-time, you know,
1.tip: 食べられる expresses ability here, and the description continues into キャンペーン on the next line.

2.lit: Since they were running a promotion, because it caught my interest a little, I came.
2.tip: 気になった means it caught the speaker's interest here, not that it worried them.

3.lit: So, I eat this, you see, but…
3.tip: 頂く is a humble word for eating; unlike the supplied translation, the Japanese does not explicitly say having already tried it.

4.lit: Well, as for taste, you know, ordinary Sapporo Ichiban and the like, that kind of, you know,
4.tip: サッポロ一番 is one brand name, offered with とか as an example of the instant ramen mentioned next.

5.lit: It is a taste of the same kind as instant ramen, you know.
5.tip: と同じような means similar to, giving a looser comparison than saying two things are exactly identical.
